items.good: Every file opens with what it is and why: each Python module with a docstring, pyproject.toml and the workflow with a comment. Every function says what it takes in and gives back, with type hints, and when it stops (main: status 1 or argparse's 2; find_organized_folder and _download_folder_named_in: FolderNotFound and when). Every test's name is one sentence of what must happen, and its body has Given/When/Then comments in plain words, so I found what each part is for before reading any body.

The tool imports only the standard library (argparse, os, platform, sys, textwrap, pathlib, re, typing) and declares no dependencies; it uses nothing newer than 3.10 (`str | None` is 3.10). I ran the T3 Test command (53 tests OK on 3.13), and the workflow's own way `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` under Python 3.10.22 with the tool installed (53 OK). The workflow runs both 3.10 and 3.x on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. git ls-remote shows that actions/checkout v7 and actions/setup-python v7 exist.

I ran the installed command with HOME set to a temporary home and hit each stop. With no settings file, a settings file naming $HOME, a settings file naming a missing folder, a given path that does not exist, and a given plain file, each stop is one line on stderr with status 1. Each names the path, says what was wrong ('cannot read ... (No such file or directory)', 'names your home folder itself', 'does not exist', 'is not a folder') and ends with 'give the folder to organize last: organize-downloads <folder>'. Doing that cleared each stop: a run given a folder listed it with status 0. An unreadable folder stops with '(Permission denied): check that you may read it, or give another folder last', and after chmod the same run listed with status 0. A wrong option stops through argparse with usage and status 2. The given folder is checked to be a folder before it is scanned, and only settings values in the forms $HOME/... or /... are used.

parts.good: The opening comment says who reads the file and where the design is. The comments say why setuptools>=77 (license as an SPDX name), why requires-python is >=3.10, and that there are no dependencies.
Says what the package does and that the command starts in cli.main.

The module docstring says it is the one part that meets the user and that --help is written from Type table. _HELP_WIDTH says why RawDescriptionHelpFormatter is used. Each function's docstring gives its inputs, output and stops: main's exit statuses, _shown's escaping of surrogates as \xNN and of unprintable characters. Names (organized, moves, _print_moves, _stop, _shown) say what they hold.

The opening explains xdg-user-dirs and why the settings file is read rather than the command run. The regular expression is explained line by line: quoting, backslash escapes, and that comments name no folder. The docstrings say how $HOME and full paths are read, why bytes are decoded with fsdecode, and each condition that stops.

Says the table is fixed and written here alone, why the extensions are in lower case and in help order, and whose endings DOWNLOADING_ENDINGS are (Chrome, Firefox, Safari). last_extension says what it gives for a name with no dot or nothing after the dot.
Says why planning is kept apart from moving. plan_moves lists every kind of entry it leaves in place, why the result is sorted, and its OSError stop.
Comments say why it runs on both systems and two Pythons, why fail-fast is off, why the tool is installed with pipx (the stories) and why the module tests use PYTHONPATH=src.

The module says how each test calls cli.main, that the planner is replaced only where a test says why, and how the no-folder test keeps off the user's home. The comments say why the unreadable-folder test is skipped for root and why the bytes test hands the name in place of the planner (macOS refuses such names). Each test name states its behavior.

The module says how each test hands its own home and system name. FOLDER_NAME_CHARACTERS says which characters are included and left out and why. FAILED_FOLDER_NAMES says what to append. shell_escaped and assertSameFolder say what they do. The comment in the no-download-folder test says why unquoted and relative forms name no folder.
Only the build backend, metadata and the one console script the README's install needs.
A docstring only; no code beyond what the package needs.

One optional folder argument (AC6), the listing (AC1), stops, and --help from Type table (the user story on reading extensions and left-in-place entries in the terminal). There is no --apply or undo yet, which T4/T5 add. _shown is needed: names with line breaks or bad bytes are shown on one line, and tests hold it.

Each branch serves AC6 or the recorded decision on Linux settings: a given folder, macOS ~/Downloads, the Linux settings with $HOME or a full path, and stops for missing, empty or home-naming settings. system and home are parameters so tests can give both systems without touching the user's home.
The AC3 table, the AC5 endings and three small lookups, each used by the planner or the help.
One function and one record type, each condition in it named in AC5.
Only the matrix AC7 and the Python decision ask for, the pipx install the stories need, and the test run.
Each test holds a behavior of the listing run, its stops or how names are shown; the helper run_main and the base class are used by all.
Each test holds one folder-finding behavior or stop. FAILED_FOLDER_NAMES is the kept-failures list B-6 asks for.

items.did: Read each module for knowledge written twice. Ran `git status --porcelain --ignored organize-downloads` after the test runs: build/, *.egg-info, and both __pycache__ folders show as ignored ('!!'), so that part holds. Looked for where the command's name is written.
items.lacking: The command's name is held in cli.PROGRAM (cli.py:18, used as argparse's prog and before every stop) and again as a literal in folder._GIVE_A_FOLDER, 'give the folder to organize last: organize-downloads <folder>' (folder.py:14). Changing PROGRAM leaves every Folder finder stop telling the user to type the old command. The name is written in two places in the code itself, apart from the console-script name in pyproject.toml, which must be there. The rest held: the type table is in type_table.py alone, the stop action in one constant, and the files a run makes are ignored.

items.did: Ran coverage.py with --branch over the whole test run: 100% of statements and branches. Copied the project to a mktemp folder and ran mutmut there through uv, leaving out test_stories.py: its source-versus-installed check fails on every mutant because mutmut's copy differs from the installed one, and nothing in the repository says so. Of 273 mutants, 204 were killed and 69 survived. Read each surviving diff with `mutmut show`. Some survivors change no behavior (follow_symlinks=None, codec names in other letter case, last_extension giving 'XXXX' in place of '' for a name with no dot), so I set those aside.
items.lacking: Mutants that change behavior survive with nothing written that says the gap was decided. (1) cli.py:32 with platform.system() replaced by None (mutmut x_main__mutmut_5) survives. The cli test with no folder given makes a home that names Downloads both the macOS and the Linux way, so no test fails when main stops passing the real system's name. On macOS with no user-dirs file, the run would then stop instead of listing ~/Downloads, which breaks AC6. (2) folder.py:78 with "$HOME" mutated (x__download_folder_named_in__mutmut_19/20) survives. Settings naming $HOME then give the 'names no download folder' stop instead of the 'names your home folder itself' stop, and test_folder.py:219-229 asserts only that the settings path is in the message, not which condition is named. The given-path stops' prefixes ('the Downloads folder ', 'the download folder <settings> names, ', mutants 13, 20-22, 36 of find_organized_folder) are not held either. (3) The output around the listing is held by no test. 'No file to move in <folder>.' replaced by None (x__print_moves__mutmut_2/4) survives, because test_cli.py:89-97 checks only that no move line is printed. The trailing 'Nothing was moved.' line (mutmut 22-25) and the plural 'N files' heading (mutmut_7, always 'file') survive too. (4) --help is built on every run but its text is never checked: 33 mutants in _parser and _help_epilog survive. These include the column width +2 changed to -2 or +3, the wrap width dropped, and the folder argument's help removed, so the help no longer showing every AC3 extension under its folder, or the left-in-place rules, would fail no test.

items.good: Each test makes its own temporary folder and cleans it up through addCleanup. The unreadable folder's permission is restored before its folder is removed (LIFO cleanup). The no-folder test patches HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME only within mock.patch.dict, so no state is left for the next test and none needs another to run first. The test with no folder given makes a home named both ways, so it holds whatever system runs it. A random property test that fails reports its input through subTest and has a list to keep it in. I ran the T3 Test command twice (and once under 3.10): 53 OK each time, so no check is already failing. A failing CLI test names one behavior: the left-in-place test checks each name with its own assertNotIn, and the planner's unit tests (each kind of entry its own test) say which rule broke.

The whole run of 53 tests took 0.089 s (1.1 s with uv's build), and mutmut ran its 273 mutants at about 390 a second. The cli and folder tests set up with tempfile and plain file writes, and run no other program.

A run only reads. It scans the folder and reads the settings file, and writes no file, folder or port, so two runs at once do not meet. I compared `ls -lAR` of a temporary home before and after a run and found nothing changed. Each test works in its own TemporaryDirectory, so parallel test workers share no place.
